FURTHER OBSERVATIONS ON 
KALA-AZAR. 
By SARATSASI KUNDU, 
Assistant Surgeon, Noivgong. 
The popularity of intravenous treatment is 
increasing daily at Nowgong; kala-azar cases 
are coming under treatment in increasing numbers, and we get the best chance of studying 
the disease more thoroughly. At present 45 
cases are attending the out-door dispensary, and 
16 cases the in-door for the treatment. The 
drawback to the work?the irregular attendance 
at the hospital owing to improvement after a few 
injections?is fading gradually, and the people 
are appreciating the efficacy of this method of 
treatment, which requires from 18-25 injections 
distributed over two to three months, and are 
attending the hospital more regularly and systematically than before. 
It is a very important point to recognise the 
appearance of the disease. It is improper to 
expect in all cases to find a typical picture of 
the disease as detailed in many text-books? 
skin and bone, witlr protuberant abdomen, oedema

of feet, great emaciation, and anaemia. The 
clinical features of kala-azar vary with the stages; 
nothing can be set as a type characteristic of the 
disease. 
(1) In the initial stage, some form of fever 
appears as the only symptom without any reaction to quinine at all. In one case we found a 
reaction to quinine, with temporary improvement 
in health,?the man thought himself perfectly 
well after 21 days of fever (with a diagnosis of 
malaria). He was again attacked with fever for 
15 days, with enlargement of spleen, and no reaction to quinine this time, a month after the 
first attack, and the man then had intravenous 
injection of antimony tartrate. He was perfectly 
cured after a course of 25 injections. He had 
occasional epistaxis and bleeding from the gums.

(2) The fever, in the intermediate stages, continues for some days or months with or without 
slight enlargement of liver and spleen; general weakness and emaciation are the only 
physical characters. We did not have cases admitted like this in the hospital, but had many 
occasions to observe these outside in private 
houses. It is interesting to note that cases of 
this kind yield very rapidly to treatment by the 
intravenous method. 
(3) As the cases become chronic and advanced, they make many different pictures :? 
(i) some with hardly any splenic enlargement, 
no noticeable enlargement of liver, and not 
much anasmia even; (ii) some with ankylostome infection and marked anaemia, but little 
enlargement of spleen and none of liver; (iii) 
some with chronic irregular fever and marked 
anaemia, but no enlargement of any organ; (iv) 
some with complications of diarrhoea or dysentery 
and with very little enlargement of spleen and 
liver; (v) some (in an almost hopeless condition) 
with profound anaemia, great emaciation, marked 
weakness, enormous enlargement of the spleen 
and often of the liver, oedema of the extremities, 
and, rarely, ascites; (vi) some with some form 
of complication,?diarrhoea, dysentery, bronchitis, pneumonia, cancrum-oris, epistaxis, otitis 
media, general oedema or ascites. In hospital 
we find these different types of cases admitted in 
the advanced stages more commonly than those 
in other stages. Cases at these stages require 
careful treatment and take a long time to-be 
thoroughly cured. 
Cardiac irritability is a marked clinical feature 
in all kala-azar cases and needs careful watching 
during treatment by the intravenous method; an 
accident occurred in a patient who was apparently 
well on the way to recovery, due to sudden 
heart failure after the injection of a large dose. 
Peculiar pigmentation of the skin, ungratified 
appetite, dryness and roughness of the body

surface, and thinning of the scalp hairs are 
noticed in some thoroughly established cases. 
Some are of opinion that oedema is a sign of 
approaching death although general conditions 
seem no worse than before. In my short experience I find it is not so. CEdema is found in 
cases of extreme ansemia and also in failing circulation. I found it to disappear in all my cases 
with a few intravenous injections of antimony 
tartrate supplemented by tonics. But oedema 
appearing in course of treatment is a signal to 
be more careful about the treatment and the 
patient; death was known to occur either with 
appearance of diarrhoea or cardiac trouble. 
Two cases of ascites with fever and enlarged 
liver and spleen were treated satisfactorily and 
successfully by repeated tappings and tartar 
emetic intravenously. These cases could not be 
confirmed by spleen puncture but were clinically 
diagnosed as kala-azar. 
It is worth while mentioning here that at the 
beginning of an attack of kala-azar after a typical 
course of pyrexia for some time, a period of 
apyrexia with general improvement for a month 
or more is noticed in some cases. It is quite 
natural for the sufferer to think he is perfectly 
cured, when again, to his surprise, fever occurs 
with other manifestation of kala-azar. In 
this way spells of fever and apyrexia recur for 
months alternating with each other, until a low 
form of irregular fever becomes persistent 
when the disease becomes thoroughly established. At Nowgong we met with cases like this 
who refused treatment intravenously at the 
beginning, on improving with general treatment, 
but afterwards submitted to the full course of 
intravenous treatment by antimony tartrate. 
Diagnosis is an essential factor in the treatment of kala-azar as a great deal depends 
on the recognition of the disease. The typical 
picture with all the clinical features is not 
common in all cases in every stage; so, for 
definite diagnosis L. D. bodies should be

searched for and detected in the blood. It 
is a difficult task to find the parasite in the 
peripheral blood. The spleen cannot be punctured in all cases as it is not possible to get 
enlargement at the beginning. No typical peculiarities of the disease can be expected in the 
early stage, with the exception of fever. Moreover, no particular type of fever is found 
characteristic especially in the early stage. So 
the refusal to react to quinine is the only peculiarity noticeable for diagnostic purposes. The 
double daily rise of temperature was thought to 
be a peculiarity in early kala-azar, but in my 
short experience it is a rarity here. Cases coming 
under treatment are more common with?(1) 
Irregular fever; (2) Intermittent fever; (3) 
Remittent fever; (4) Continued fever; (5) 
Rheumatic fever; (6) Fever like malarial rigor;

and (7) Fever suspected as typhoid. So it is 
an extremely difficult task to give a positive 
diagnosis at the early stage by simply watching 
the course of fever,, and at the same time it is 
rash to pronounce the case as kala-azar without 
having found the L. D. bodies in the blood. 
I am of opinion that every case with chronic 
irregular fever, progressive emaciation and weakness, gradual enlargement of spleen and liver, and 
resistance to ordinary doses of quinine by mouth 
and injections, should be looked upon with great 
suspicion and treated as kala-azar considering 
the locality. In this connection it should be noted 
that we had many cases of this type outside the 
hospital, and when intravenous injections of antimony tartrate were started and continued, these 
were found to improve and become thoroughly 
cured. When a case with splenic enlargement is 
met with, if possible spleen puncture should be 
performed for definite diagnosis, and only cases 
with a positive examination should be declared

as kala-azar. 
Spleen puncture is generally done with the 
utmost aseptic precaution throughout the operation. No fatality has been known. A few had 
pain over the site of puncture (for a day omy), 
but no rise of temperature was seen in any case 
due to operation. 
Parasites are found either free or in leucocytes, 
but the tree forms are more common and in the 
stage of full development; smaller or younger 
forms are seldom seen outside the leucocytes. 
They exhibit different types in respect of 
shape?(i) some elongated and pointed at one 
end like a torpedo; (11) some pointed at both 
ends and shaped like a boat; (iii) some large 
and oval; (iv) some big and round like a ball. 
It is worthy of mention that the film prepared 
from the splenic blood of a case of mixed 
intection of ankylostome and leishmania gave a 
most beautiful picture of the parasite; each 
leishmania was sufficiently big and round to be 
compared with a red cell. 
Many eminent physicians consider spleen 
puncture unnecessary for diagnosis, but the risks 
are so small that this, in view especially of the 
difficulty of finding the parasite in the peripheral 
blood, seems to me a justifiable procedure for 
positive diagnosis. 
Modes of infection.?These have not been definitely ascertained by any one. I see that the 
probable modes of infection, as cherished by 
specialists, are many. There is no conclusive 
proof for or against each theory,?sources of 
infection are not limited to any one group, and 
chances of transmission are equal to all agents. 
(1) One theory is that of insect or animal infection. Bed-bugs, mosquitoes, house-flies, lice 
and ticks, fleas, and dogs?these bring about the I infection and spread of the disease either by | 
biting and so injecting, or depositing the infecting 
material on the skin, the absorption of the infection taking place by cutaneous lymphatics. 
(2) Another theory is of oral ingestion.

Leishmania is possibly ingested by food contaminated by excreta or other substances containing the encysted forms of the flagellate, and the 
infection takes place through the mucous membrane of the intestinal tract. 
(3) Another theory is of ankylostome infection. Infected ankylostome ova are passed with 
the faeces, these mature and live as worms on the 
earth, and the infection takes place by the entrance of the infected worms through the feet 
or any other part of the body. 
At Nowgong kala-azar is more common among 
the natives of the place, specially among the 
cultivators and villagers, rare among the Bengalees, and not much known among the Keyas. 
This last named class of people are always coming 
in contact with the Assamese and constantly 
mixing with them throughout the district. On 
the other hand, they are strict vegetarians and 
their principal substance of diet is " 
ghee." But 
the Assamese and the others mainly depend on 
fish for their diet. All the facts taken together 
lead me to suggest the probability of fish-infection. Fish may become infected by eating 
the infected excreta or substances containing 
the encysted flagellates from infected places 
generally visited by the carrier, and the leishmania may get entrance into the human body 
through the infected fish in the diet. On the 
other hand, the fatty substance 
" 
ghee 
" in the 
Keyas may act as a prophylactic agent against 
kala-azar. This is a mere suggestion which 
arises in my mind from the observation of the 
cases coming from the villages. I cannot 
study it thoroughly as I cannot devote my 
whole time to its investigation. It is essentially the work of a research scholar who 
has all his time at his command for making a 
thorough and lengthy observation and carrying 
out the difficult but important problem of tracing 
out the sources of transmission from man to 
man. 
Another peculiarity I notice here is that in

some houses one and rarely two cases of kalaazar, either in the early stage or in the advanced 
condition, were found in a family of several 
healthy members. Household infection is not a 
marked feature in this town during these days, 
but in the recently notified area family infection 
is found very common as the disease breaks out 
in epidemic form there. 
Our Civil Surgeon, Dr. Dodds Price, sent 
some months ago a family of six members from 
a garden for treatment of kala-azar. Three of 
them?the father aged 45, the wife aged 35, and 
the adult girl aged 14?were ill; but the three

children?a boy aged 7, a boy aged 4, and another 
aged 2?were in perfect good health?no sign 
of any illness was detected among them. The 
father complained of diarrhoea and anaemia but 
no spleen and died suddenly within two days of 
admission into hospital. The wife and the 
daughter had ankylostome infection with leishmaniasis, enlarged spleen and marked anaemia, 
but liver just palpable. Spleen puncture of these 
two gave a most beautiful picture of the parasite, 
in the big and round shape. This is an instance 
of house infection among adults but rare in the 
children. The girl died with intense anaemia, 
and with the complication of diarrhoea. The 
mother was thoroughly cured after a course 
of treatment for three months. 
As already detailed, the patient is treated by 
intravenous injection of antimony tartrate supplemented by some form of tonic, but no arsenic 
in any form is given as it is found contraindicated along with antimony. No other 
method is found to be so efficacious as this. We 
tried here antimony oxide in pill form in two 
cases only, and we had no occasion to try it 
intravenously; but the results were not successful, and we had to stop it, as we found the 
intravenous injection of antimony tartrate most

successful and efficacious. Particular care should 
be taken to obtain a clear, fresh and sterile 
solution since accidents are liable to occur if 
this rule is disobeyed; even death is quite possible, with hyperpyrexia and collapse, within a 
few hours after the injection of old solution 
which acts as a poison in the system. 
Generally the patient takes the injection sitting 
on a bench, but it is urged by some to confine 
the patient to bed on the day of injection, and 
till the day after. I do not find this so important. We had many cases in the out-door 
who came walking from three or four miles' 
distance and left the hospital again after the 
injection. I did not find any fatality or danger 
occurring amongst them. If inflammation was 
found in any case at the site of injection, 
ichthyol-belladonna application was found sufficient to suppress all symptoms and remove the 
complication. 
In my last paper I noted the two unpleasant 
symptoms coughing and vomiting occurring with 
a big dose as the stage of cure was approached. 
Fainting and hyperpyrexia were also observed in 
some of the out-door cases just after the injection, and on these a strict watch was kept with 
the next higher dose. Also I detailed the 
toxic action of the drug. Accidents were reported in the advanced stage of treatment,?in 
one, diarrhoea set in with rapid loss of flesh 
and depression, resulting in collapse and death. 
In two, death occurred suddenly with a fit of an 
epileptic nature when they were apparently well 
after a sufficient number of injections, and were 
about to be discharged cured from the hospital. 
In another case where the patient was improving 
with a number of injections, a feeling of constriction within the chest was complained of just 
after the injection of a large dose, the heart became irritable and painful, and the patient died 
soon after. These were probably due to heart 
failure. So, owing to the cardiac irritability in 
kala-azar, the state of the heart should be carefully watched and studied and the treatment

should be continued cautiously so as to avoid 
these dangerous accidents. All these facts taken 
together lead me to suspect the cumulation of 
the drug in the tissues; so before it is excreted 
completely from the system, no repetition of 
the drug should be given as no tolerance for 
antimony can be expected in weak, anaemic and 
debilitated bodies. 
As a rule a febrile reaction was noticed in all 
cases at the commencement of treatment, but 
with some a fall in temperature was often 
found after the antimony injections instead of 
reaction. Febrile reaction becomes more marked 
when a medium dose of 4 to 6 c.c. is given to 
a patient. Spleen, as detailed in the last paper, 
disappears with the course of treatment. About 
the liver I noticed the fact that it did not disappear with spleen and fever. It is the last 
organ which assumes the normal condition after 
treatment. Some physicians advocate the intramuscular injection of a preparation of turpentine, creosote, and camphor for the enlargement 
of spleen. We had no occasion to try this. 
We find in most cases that the spleen disappears 
rapidly and easily with the continuance of 
treatment. Is it then a necessary factor to be 
observed ? A peculiar skin eruption was 
found in some cases in the last stage of treatment?with the stoppage of fever. For this, 
injections were temporarily suspended and simple 
liq. Donovan was given with marked success. 
In many cases when spleen puncture was 
performed during the course of treatment, parasites were found to be present, even when fever 
had been absent for some days, and injections 
were continued. In case of non-disappearance 
of spleen under the ribs it is possible to prove 
sterilisation of the body by spleen puncture. 
But in many, spleen puncture could not be done 
owing to disappearance of the organ under the 
ribs. Here is the difficulty to determine the 
test of cure. Some eminent physicians rely on 
the absence of fever for a considerable time,

marked general improvement, and disappearance 
of spleen. At Nowgong we do not rely simply 
upon this. Our practice is to watch the patient 
for a fortnight or more without any injection, 
when we think the patient is cured. Intravenous injections are started again with a medium

dose, and if refusal to react to antimony tartrate for two or three consecutive injections is 
noticed, we take this fact as the test of cure 
and the certain sterilisation of the body. Peripheral blood also shows marked increase in 
leucocytes at the stage of cure. 
In the town we had a case in a boy of 10 years 
suffering from kala-azar. He did not take 
injections regularly and had only about 12. 
Fever did not stop completely, and the spleen 
was 5 in. below the costal margin. During 
the course of treatment he was attacked with 
double pneumonia. With the cure of this complication he was found cured completely from 
kala-azar without any further intravenous treatment. This peculiar instance suggests the inference that leishmaniasis disappears from the 
system after a virulent infection of some sort 
of pathogenic micro-organism. 
In conclusion I should like to impress that 
the intravenous use of tartar emetic is the best 
form of treatment for kala-azar cases in any 
stage, but the use of this drug needs careful 
watching and attention, and the patient requires 
special and proper care throughout the whole 
course of treatment. It must be noted that the 
drug should not be pushed to a dangerous extent 
and a careful watch should be kept to 
avoid the danger of going on too long with too 
large doses of antimony tartrate, once the 
indication of the disappearance of the parasite 
has become evident.
